summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. It stands under the United Kingdom's legal framework only where that framework is extended to it: the Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply automatically, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is lawful in Guernsey for men and women. Decriminalisation preceded 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences in its criminal law, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can therefore face prosecution for conduct that is lawful in the United Kingdom.

Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law permits only the issue of a new certificate and does not amend or remove entries from the existing record, so prior gender markers remain visible on the original document. A visitor carrying documents issued at different times should expect the earlier marker to remain on file.

The States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage on 10 December 2015 by 37 votes to 7, rejecting both a civil-partnership-only scheme and a single secular status called Union Civile as insufficient. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill, which commenced in 2018. Guernsey has never enacted its own civil partnership legislation, and United Kingdom civil partnerships have been recognised for succession purposes since 2 April 2012.

Discrimination protection was assembled in stages. A 2004 law enabled the States to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 prohibited discrimination on grounds of gender identity in employment. A 2020 snapshot records that no equivalent Ordinance had yet outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity have applied in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously, 33 votes to 0, explicitly including sexual orientation and rejecting proposed exemptions for businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations; it took effect on 1 October 2023 and now supplies the statutory protection covering sexual orientation that the Ordinance route had not delivered.

Les Nicolles, Guernsey's only prison, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages across 11 wings, with a capacity of 139 and about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded in the available sources, so a trans visitor has no sourced assurance about placement if detained.
tangentialFactors:
Guernsey adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay and bisexual men eligible to donate after a 12-month deferral with effect from about 7 November 2011 and ending a local ban dating from the 1980s HIV era; other donation restrictions were unchanged.

Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted its own civil partnership legislation, a distinction it holds alongside its recognition of United Kingdom civil partnerships for succession purposes from 2 April 2012.

Jersey approved the same removal of the bar on unmarried couples adopting two days before Guernsey did in June 2015, so the family-law change was adopted across neighbouring jurisdictions within the same week.
localsOnly:
A review of the Adoption Law, recorded at page 1170 of the Billet d'État of 24 June 2015, ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting. The States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised in adoption proceedings, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

Employment is the one field where gender-identity discrimination has been prohibited since the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005, passed under the enabling law of 2004. The comprehensive anti-discrimination statute that took effect on 1 October 2023 extends protection beyond employment and expressly covers sexual orientation, having been carried 33 votes to 0 with the proposed small-business and religious exemptions rejected.

Protection on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity in child welfare proceedings has been in force in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016, predating the general statute by years.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents border or airport screening practice in Guernsey, treatment of gender markers on entry documents, or any visa condition keyed to gender status. These remain unsourced rather than resolved.

No source records healthcare access for trans visitors, including whether gender-affirming medication requires documentation on arrival or a prescription recognised locally.

No trans-specific violent incident with a date and an outcome is documented for Guernsey in the available sources. The absence of a documented case is not evidence that none occurs.

The 2020 position on sexual-orientation discrimination Ordinances is a historical snapshot; the comprehensive statute commenced on 1 October 2023, and its enforcement record, including any decision applying it to a gender-identity claim, is not sourced here.

Whether Guernsey's criminal law treats anti-trans motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and how the prison decides placement for a trans detainee, are both unresolved in the available sources.
